analysis.productSummary: A small wall bracket (80 × 60 × 50 mm, 28 cm³, 3 mm walls) that cantilevers a 600 g e-bike charger off the garage floor. Sold to e-bike OEMs and accessory retailers. At 500 units, injection mold tooling blows the $4,000 budget; a bent sheet-metal version ships for less.
detectedFeatures: Two wall-mount screw holes in base
Two charger-mount screw holes in upright
Watertight mesh, no sub-1 mm walls

pros: Fits the $4,000 budget at 500 units with room to spare
No tooling; five local brake and laser shops can make it
Stronger than 3 mm glass-filled nylon at the gusset root
Flat blank ships and stores cheaply
cons: Needs a redraw from molded solid to flat pattern
Bare metal needs powder coat or anodize for garage humidity
Sharp edges require deburr spec
Loses the molded charger pocket contour

designTweaks.change: Re-model as one 2 mm Aluminum 5052 flat blank ~140 × 60 mm with a single 90° bend and 4 mm bend-relief notches.
designTweaks.why: One bend on a brake replaces a mold cavity entirely, and many local laser and brake shops can make it.
designTweaks.impact: Drops unit cost from ~$18 (SLS) to ~$6 and removes all tooling spend.

designTweaks.change: Replace the two 3 mm gussets with 10 mm upturned side flanges along the 60 mm edges, formed in the same setup.
designTweaks.why: Flanges stiffen the cantilever without welding or a separate part.
designTweaks.impact: Same stiffness, zero welding cost, ~$1.50/part saved versus welded gussets.

designTweaks.change: Make the two charger holes 5 mm keyhole slots and the two wall holes 5.5 mm with 4 mm edge distance.
designTweaks.why: Keyholes let the charger hang on pre-set screws; edge distance prevents tear-out at the bend.
designTweaks.impact: Eliminates one assembly step for the end user and reduces field warranty returns.

pros: Cheapest part cost long-term: under $2 at volume
Molded pocket can match the charger brick exactly
Four local presses; a 400 × 350 mm platen is ample
cons: Tooling alone exceeds the entire $4,000 budget at 500 units
6-8 week first-article lead time
GF nylon sinks and warps at 3 mm next to 3 mm gussets
Design locked once steel is cut

designTweaks.change: Thin the two gussets to 1.5 mm (60% of the 3 mm wall) and add a 1.5° draft on the 50 mm upright faces.
designTweaks.why: Gussets at full wall thickness sink on the visible outer face and slow cooling; draft frees a straight-pull tool.
designTweaks.impact: Removes sink marks and cuts cycle ~15%, avoiding any side-action (~$1,200 tooling saved).

designTweaks.change: Core the base to a uniform 2.5 mm shell with 1 mm internal ribs on 15 mm centers instead of solid sections.
designTweaks.why: Uniform wall is the single biggest driver of warp in glass-filled nylon.
designTweaks.impact: Shot weight drops ~20%, cycle time ~3 s shorter, ~$0.30/part.

designTweaks.change: Add 0.5 mm radii at both gusset-to-upright roots and counterbore the two charger holes in the mold.
designTweaks.why: Sharp roots are where a notch-sensitive GF nylon cracks under the 600 g cantilever load.
designTweaks.impact: Meaningfully raises drop/fatigue margin; removes a secondary drilling operation.

pros: Keeps the exact drawn geometry, no redesign
Zero tooling, parts in under two weeks
Isotropic nylon is genuinely strong enough for 600 g
cons: 500 units costs ~$9,000, over double the budget
Only a few local SLS machines; 165 mm chamber limits nesting
Grainy finish, needs dyeing for a retail look

designTweaks.change: Hollow the base and upright to 2.5 mm shells with two 4 mm powder-escape holes on the hidden underside.
designTweaks.why: SLS is priced mostly by material volume and packed build height.
designTweaks.impact: Cuts volume ~30%, roughly $4-6 off each part.

designTweaks.change: Orient the part with the 50 mm upright along Z and pack 40+ per build in the 165 mm chamber.
designTweaks.why: Nesting density is the other half of SLS unit cost.
designTweaks.impact: ~20% lower per-part cost versus loose single-part builds.

designTweaks.change: Print the four screw holes 0.4 mm undersize and spec heat-set M4 inserts in the two charger holes.
designTweaks.why: SLS holes close slightly and self-tapping into nylon strips after a few cycles.
designTweaks.impact: Reliable re-serviceable mounting; ~$0.60/part insert cost.

pros: Six local mill shops, fast quotes
Aluminum version is essentially unbreakable at 76 g
Good for a premium or OEM-branded SKU
cons: 12% box fill means ~88% of the billet is chips
Needs 2-3 setups plus a soft-jaw fixture
~$11,000 for 500 units, far over budget

designTweaks.change: Machine from 50.8 mm 6061 plate with a flat back face, so the part runs in two setups on standard soft jaws.
designTweaks.why: A flat datum face lets one vise hold the base while the upright and gussets are cut.
designTweaks.impact: Removes a third setup, roughly 20% of unit cost.

designTweaks.change: Open all internal corners to 6 mm radius and replace the two gussets with a single 12 mm fillet.
designTweaks.why: A 12 mm endmill can then rough the whole pocket at full depth without small-tool passes.
designTweaks.impact: Cycle time down ~25%, about $5/part at 500.

designTweaks.change: Pocket the base underside to a 5 mm floor with 8 mm ribs instead of leaving it solid.
designTweaks.why: Less billet mass and lighter stock reduces both material and cycle cost.
designTweaks.impact: ~15% material saving and a lighter shipping weight.

analysis.topRecommendation: Redraw this as a bent 2 mm aluminum 5052 L-bracket and have a local laser and brake shop make 500 for roughly $3,000 delivered, inside budget with no tooling. Keep the molded glass-filled nylon design on the shelf and cut steel when your committed order reaches about 2,000-2,500 units, where the $3,000-7,000 tool pays back.
risks: At 500 units the injection-mold path costs $4,000-9,000 in tooling alone, before a single part, which breaks the stated budget.
No photos or charger dimensions were supplied, so the 60 mm-wide pocket and the two charger screw holes may not match the real brick.
Glass-filled nylon is notch-sensitive: the sharp gusset-to-upright roots are the likely crack site under a 600 g cantilevered load plus cable tug.
Two screws into drywall will pull out under 600 g plus cable load; the product needs specified anchors or a stud-spacing hole pattern.
A 3 mm wall meeting 3 mm gussets in 30% GF nylon will sink and warp unless the gussets are thinned before the tool is cut.

analysis.productSummary: A 2 mm aluminum 5052 wall bracket that lifts a ~600 g e-bike charger brick off the garage floor: one flat blank, one 90° bend, four screw holes. It is now a pure laser-and-brake part, so 500 units need no tooling and land near $6 each.
detectedFeatures: Two wall-mount screw holes in base
4 mm bend-relief notches at bend ends
Uniform 2 mm wall, no gussets or ribs

pros: One bend, one blank: cheapest possible route at 500 units
Zero hard tooling; fits the $4,000 budget with room
Three local brake and punch shops can make it
5052 bends cleanly at 2 mm without cracking
cons: Setup cost dominates below ~50 pieces
2 mm unribbed upright may flex under a 600 g cantilever
Bend angle tolerance ±1° affects wall fit
Cosmetic finish needs a separate tumble or anodize step

designTweaks.change: Lengthen the upright's rear edge into a 10 mm return flange folded the same direction, adding a second bend on the same brake setup.
designTweaks.why: A 2 mm 5052 upright with no gussets is the weak point under a 600 g offset load.
designTweaks.impact: Roughly triples upright stiffness for about $0.40/part and no new tooling.

designTweaks.change: Change the two wall holes to 5.5 × 11 mm slots and keep all holes ≥8 mm from the bend line.
designTweaks.why: Slots absorb stud-spacing error; holes too near the bend distort during forming.
designTweaks.impact: Eliminates field drilling complaints and scrapped parts from oval holes.

designTweaks.change: Nest the ~140 × 60 mm blanks on common lines with 3 mm corner radii on a 1220 × 2440 sheet.
designTweaks.why: Shared cut lines and radii cut pierce count and laser travel per blank.
designTweaks.impact: ~15-20% less cut time and about 10% better material yield.

pros: Five local laser shops; blanks in under a week
No tooling at all, fastest quote turnaround
Holes, slots and relief notches cut in one hit
cons: Flat blank only; forming must be bought separately
Adds a vendor handoff and extra freight leg
Cut edges on aluminum need deburring before folding

designTweaks.change: Add two 3 mm tooling holes on the base centerline, 100 mm apart, outside the screw pattern.
designTweaks.why: Gives the brake operator a hard locating datum instead of scribing the bend line.
designTweaks.impact: Cuts bend setup time and holds leg length within ±0.3 mm.

designTweaks.change: Etch the bend line and part revision as a 0.2 mm laser score on the inside face.
designTweaks.why: Prevents mis-folded parts when blanks move between two shops.
designTweaks.impact: Near-zero cost, removes a common 2-5% scrap cause on split-vendor jobs.

designTweaks.change: Order blanks in tabbed sheets of 10 rather than loose parts.
designTweaks.why: Reduces handling and part-count fees at the laser and during transport.
designTweaks.impact: Saves roughly $0.30-0.60 per part at 500 units.

pros: No bend-angle variation; sharp repeatable 90°
Can be cut as a solid angle for maximum stiffness
Six local mill shops, easy to source
cons: 3-4x the sheet metal unit cost at 500 units
Wastes ~90% of the plate stock as chips
Needs a soft-jaw fixture for the second face

designTweaks.change: Mill from 2 mm extruded 6061 angle stock instead of plate, machining only the holes and outline.
designTweaks.why: Buying the 90° as stock removes most of the metal removal and one setup.
designTweaks.impact: Drops unit cost to roughly $9-14 and halves cycle time.

designTweaks.change: Fixture 6 parts per vise setup using a common 3 mm dowel pattern in the base.
designTweaks.why: Load/unload time, not cutting, dominates cost on a 45 g part.
designTweaks.impact: ~30% lower unit cost at 500 pieces.

designTweaks.change: Drop any countersinks; use pan-head screws with straight 5.5 mm clearance holes.
designTweaks.why: Countersinks add a tool change and second operation for no functional gain.
designTweaks.impact: Removes ~15 seconds of cycle time per part.

pros: Good for 5-20 fit-check samples before committing the blank
No tooling, next-day parts from six local machines
cons: Layer lines run across the bend corner: the weakest direction
Garage heat and UV degrade most FDM plastics over time
Cost never falls below ~$6; shops cap at 1,000 units
Creep under a sustained 600 g load

designTweaks.change: Print with the L-corner flat on the bed so layers run along, not across, the loaded corner.
designTweaks.why: FDM parts fail along layer boundaries at the inside radius of an L.
designTweaks.impact: Two to three times higher failure load with no cost change.

designTweaks.change: Add a 6 mm triangular gusset at the inside corner and a 5 mm inside fillet.
designTweaks.why: Plastic cannot match 2 mm aluminum stiffness without added section.
designTweaks.impact: Makes a printed prototype usable for real load testing.

designTweaks.change: Thicken walls to 4 mm and use brass heat-set inserts at the charger holes.
designTweaks.why: Screws into 2 mm printed plastic strip out on first install.
designTweaks.impact: Adds ~$1.50/part but removes the main prototype failure mode.

analysis.topRecommendation: Yes, the revision worked: one flat blank, one bend and relief notches puts this squarely in sheet metal at roughly $4.50-$7.50 per part with no hard tooling, about $3,000 for 500 and inside budget. Buy laser-cut blanks and forming from one shop. Only at 25,000+ units would a progressive die or molded PA66 bracket beat it.
risks: A 2 mm 5052 upright with no gussets may flex or fatigue under a 600 g charger cantilevered off the wall; load-test three parts before releasing 500.
Mounting relies on two screws into the charger housing, whose plastic bosses may not be rated to carry the brick's weight.
Holes placed closer than ~8 mm to the bend line will distort during forming and cause assembly fit problems.
The 80 × 60 × 50 mm folded envelope implies ~50 mm of upright; confirm it actually clears your charger body and cable exit.
Bend angle on 5052 typically varies ±1°, so a bracket that is square on the CAD may sit slightly off the wall.

listing.title: E-Bike Charger Wall Bracket, Aluminum Garage Wall Mount Holder for Charger Brick, Bike Storage Organizer
listing.description:
A simple wall-mount bracket that gets your e-bike charger brick off the garage floor and out of the way. Made from a single piece of 2 mm aluminum 5052-H32, laser cut and folded with one 90 degree bend. No plastic clips, no flex.

Good for e-bike owners, retrofit riders and anyone tidying a garage wall, workshop or bike corner.

- Holds a charger brick of roughly 600 g
- Folded size: 80 x 60 x 50 mm
- Cut from a flat blank about 140 x 60 mm, 2 mm thick
- Two screw holes in the base for mounting to the wall
- Two screw holes in the upright to attach the charger
- 4 mm bend-relief notches at each end of the bend
- Uniform 2 mm wall, no gussets or ribs, easy to wipe clean

Material: aluminum 5052-H32, 2 mm. Raw mill finish.

Please check your charger's mounting holes and size before ordering, as hole spacing is fixed.

In the box:
- 1 aluminum charger wall bracket

Screws are not included, since the right wall anchor depends on your wall. Drywall, stud, brick and block all take different hardware.

items.name: Bracket body
items.spec: Aluminum 5052-H32, 2.0 mm sheet; ~140 × 60 mm flat blank, laser cut, one 90° bend to 80 × 60 × 50 mm envelope; 4 mm bend-relief notches; 3 mm corner radii; 4 holes, deburred.
items.notes: Confirm hole-to-bend distance is at least 8 mm so holes don't distort during forming.

items.spec: Nylon expansion plug for masonry, 8 mm drill diameter, suits 5 mm screw, 40 mm length.
items.notes: Include only if you ship a masonry-ready kit; drywall garages need toggles instead.

items.name: Charger mount screw
items.spec: ISO 7380 button head M4 × 12, A2 stainless, hex socket.
items.notes: Confirm thread and length against the charger's own mounting bosses.

items.name: Nylon-insert lock nut
items.spec: ISO 10511 thin nylon-insert lock nut M4, A2 stainless.
items.notes: Drop this line if the charger has tapped holes rather than through-holes.

items.name: Flat washer
items.spec: ISO 7089 flat washer M4, A2 stainless, 200 HV.

items.name: Self-adhesive cushion pad
items.spec: Closed-cell EPDM foam strip, 2 mm thick, ~50 × 50 mm, acrylic pressure-sensitive adhesive backing, black.
items.notes: Protects the charger case and damps rattle; die-cut to shape at volume.

items.name: Powder coat
items.spec: Chromate-free pretreatment plus polyester powder coat, matte black RAL 9005, 60–80 µm, masking of the four screw holes not required.
items.notes: Clear anodize is an alternative if you prefer a bare-metal look; price similarly.

items.name: Printed carton

items.notes: State the load rating and fixings needed for each wall type.

assumptions: Assumed the charger mounts with M4 screws through existing holes; confirm before finalising fastener lines.
Assumed the product ships as a kit with wall fixings for masonry, which is the common garage case.
Assumed a painted finish is wanted for a garage environment; bare 5052 would work but marks easily.
Assumed no return flange is added; if the second bend is adopted, blank length and part price rise slightly.
